hints: Focus on what hot NaOH does to chlorine, as bromine will do the same thing here with warm NaOH.
Recall the disproportionation to chloride (-1) and chlorate(V) (+5), so write the balanced equation for bromine forming bromide and bromate(V).
Identify the Na, Br, O product as sodium bromate(V), find its moles from 30.2 g, then use the 6 to 1 NaOH to bromate ratio to get mass.
walkthrough:
**Recall the chlorine with hot NaOH reaction**

Chlorine disproportionates in hot concentrated NaOH to oxidation states -1 and +5. This is the model for bromine.

$$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Write the matching bromine equation**

Bromine does the same with warm NaOH, giving bromide (-1) and bromate(V) (+5) in the same 5 to 1 ratio.

$$3\text{Br}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaBr} + \text{NaBrO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Find moles of the Na-Br-O product**

The product containing Na, Br and O must be $\text{NaBrO}_3$, sodium bromate(V), not $\text{NaBr}$.

$$M_r(\text{NaBrO}_3) = 23.0 + 79.9 + 3(16.0) = 150.9$$
$$n(\text{NaBrO}_3) = \frac{30.2}{150.9} \approx 0.200 \text{ mol}$$

**Use the mole ratio to find NaOH**

From the equation, 6 mol NaOH makes 1 mol $\text{NaBrO}_3$.

$$n(\text{NaOH}) = 6 \times 0.200 = 1.20 \text{ mol}$$
$$m(\text{NaOH}) = 1.20 \times 40.0 = 48.0 \text{ g}$$

options.A: Incorrect. 8.00 g is 0.200 mol of NaOH, which assumes a 1 to 1 ratio of NaOH to NaBrO3. The balanced disproportionation equation needs 6 mol NaOH for every 1 mol NaBrO3.
options.B: Incorrect. About 10.2 g comes from two mistakes: using the cold NaOH product NaOBr (hypobromite, Br +1) instead of the warm product NaBrO3, and then using a 1 to 1 ratio instead of 2 NaOH to 1 NaOBr.
options.C: Incorrect. 20.3 g is the answer for the cold NaOH reaction: Br2 + 2NaOH gives NaOBr. Moles of NaOBr = 30.2 / 118.9 = 0.254 mol, giving 0.508 mol NaOH. This question specifies warm NaOH, which gives bromate(V), not hypobromite.
options.D: Correct. 30.2 g of NaBrO3 is 0.200 mol. The hot/warm disproportionation requires 6 NaOH per NaBrO3, so 1.20 mol NaOH reacts, which is 48.0 g.
